wtf is with you people trying to take away one of the only places for dogs to access water within the city? Yes dogs can access the river. Go somewhere else if you don’t like dogs!

I was downtown yesterday evening and was happily surprised by how vibrant things seemed. It was a very good vibe. Salsa dancing at river landing, lots of people at pubs and restaurants, and just a gorgeous evening. 

I work downtown and yeah, sketchy folks walk past my office window but generally I really like working downtown. There's so many great restaurants for cheap lunches and I love being close to the river. I can go for a run or a walk along the river so easily. I bike so the traffic issues have mostly not affected me.

I'm right on the edge of Holiday Park and King George. Spend a lot of time in Holiday Park on foot. Quiet area. Lots of access to green space and the river. Gordie Howe sports complex right there. Easy access to downtown, even via bus in under 15 minutes usually. 

The only real downside is no grocery store, for more than basic items you'll have to head to confed. In a pinch Victoria Fine Foods on 11th might have what you're after. There is a Market of Asia on 11th as well, between Holiday Park and Montgomery. 

Safe enough to leave windows open when you're home? Is there an area in Saskatoon you can't do that? Asking as someone who's lived in... 7 or 8 neighborhoods in the last 25 years. You can absolutely leave your windows open when you're home in Holiday Park.

Plenty of kids, working class families, a couple of retirement communities. Older homes, generally well cared for. You'll see plenty of people walking their dogs.

Going to school in Saskatoon through the 90s, I think there was a stabbing at least once a year pretty consistently (including elementary schools). One of my childhood friends got stabbed in the field behind River Heights out of school hours when he was in about grade 4-5. Someone got stabbed at least once a year at Bedford, and they wouldn't even clear the hallways when the ambulance came. It wasn't 'News' in any sense of the word.

I'm not saying any of that is good, but the hand wringing about 'kids these days' is way overwrought. Kids are demons, and schools have always been torture farms. Based on the statistics you see about youth partying (which is down across the board), I would actually guess that \*most\* kids are more well behaved now than when I was young.
I used to live on 33rd St East - just 5 blocks from the river - right across the street from the train tracks.  And honestly you get so used to it that you don't notice it.
There are public washrooms in the parks along the river, in every mall, at every public library and in every civic centre, as well as Home Depot, Co-op, Rona, Walmart, most grocery stores, etc.

In the heart of Saskatoon, near the winding path of Spadina Crescent that hugs the South Saskatchewan River, there’s a story cab drivers whisper—but only on slow, quiet nights.

Back in the late 1990s, a taxi driver named Henry was doing his usual late-night shift. Around 2:45 a.m., he was heading down Spadina Crescent when he spotted a woman standing at the edge of the road, just outside the Delta Bessborough Hotel. She wore a long coat, hair pinned up neatly, and raised her hand for a ride.

Henry pulled over.

"Where to?" he asked, glancing at her in the rearview mirror.

"Please… take me to the university bridge. My fiancé... he's waiting," she said softly.

Though the request was odd—it was a chilly March night, and no one usually walked that part of the bridge at this hour—Henry nodded and drove. As they crossed the darkened bridge, lit only by sparse lamplight and the river glinting below, he tried making small talk.

No reply.

He glanced back.
The seat was empty.
Only a faint trace of frost remained on the fabric where she had been sitting.

Panicked, Henry stopped the car in the middle of the bridge and looked around. Nothing. Not a soul in sight. He drove straight back to the Delta Hotel, where a night clerk was outside on a smoke break.

“You look like you've seen a ghost,” the clerk joked.

Henry described what happened.

The clerk paused. “That sounds like Emma. She was a young bride-to-be who died in a car crash on this bridge in 1963. Her fiancé was waiting for her at the university, but she never made it. Some say she still tries…”

Since that night, other drivers have reported the same woman, always near the Bessborough, always asking to be taken to the university bridge. No one’s ever seen her reach the other side.
